Days/week and split type come from your Training Plan settings (Settings tab).
Fixes every exercise to the same number. Left on "let AI decide", it varies sets by exercise — usually more on compounds than on isolation work. Pinning it is applied on the way in as well as asked for in the prompt, so the plan gets the number you chose whatever the model returns. With a session length set, fixing sets means the AI adjusts the number of exercises to fit instead.
Kept between generations, including next week's — an injury outlasts one plan. Everything on this form is saved as you leave each field, so clear a note once it no longer applies.
Uses your OpenRouter API key from Settings. The call goes straight from this page to OpenRouter — nothing passes through any server of mine.
Units
Everything is stored in kg internally — this only changes how weights are entered and displayed. Switching is instant and doesn't touch any logged history.
Lifter profile
Pick the one that matches what's actually happening, not how long you've been training. The standard definition of these levels is how long you need to recover enough to add load — session, week, or block — and calendar time is only a rough proxy for it: novice progression typically runs 3–9 months but people burn through it anywhere from 8 weeks to well over a year. It's also per-lift, not global — most people are still novices on overhead press long after their squat isn't. This app already detects that part on its own from your logged history.
Used only as context for AI plan generation. It deliberately does not scale how fast weight is added — meta-analysis of controlled trials finds women's relative strength gains equal to men's in the lower body and slightly greater in the upper body. What does differ is absolute load, and the load-relative increments above already account for that without needing to know your sex.
Applies a small taper to the progression rate past 40. Strength gains continue at every age — the rate and the recovery between sessions are what decline. The exact coefficients here are a judgment call, not a number lifted from a study.
Used to compute the real load on bodyweight and assisted exercises. A pull-up with +10 isn't a 10 lift, and an assisted pull-up at -45 isn't a -45 lift — without your bodyweight the percentage increments on those are computed off the wrong number entirely.
In a deficit, strength gains attenuate and holding load is a good result — so progression slows down and a session that repeats last week's numbers is reported as a win rather than a miss. Coefficients are a judgment call; the direction of the effect is well established.
Workout
2–3 min suits heavy compounds; 60–90s is plenty for isolation work. It doesn't run after the set that finishes an exercise — moving to the next machine is the rest, and you set that pace yourself.
On by default. Turned off, logging a set records it and nothing else happens — no countdown, no sheet, no beep. The timer is a tool for people who rest to a clock; it shouldn't be mandatory furniture for people who don't.
On by default. Asks once per exercise, right after you log its final prescribed set — the moment you actually know the answer. Skipping is one tap and changes nothing; the value only ever speeds progression up when you report headroom to spare.
Set per equipment type, because the jump is a property of the implement, not of you: a barbell with 1.25kg plates moves in 2.5kg steps, a dumbbell rack in 2kg or 5lb steps whatever you'd prefer, and a pin stack in 5kg steps regardless. Progression suggestions round to these, so they set the floor on how finely load can advance — and on light lifts that floor overrides your experience setting entirely. Each exercise picks up a type automatically from its name; correct any of them on the Exercises tab.
OpenRouter
Saved on this device as soon as you leave the field. Stored unencrypted in this browser's own storage; anyone with access to this browser profile can read it. Use a spend-limited OpenRouter key.
Check openrouter.ai/models for current options and pricing — not hardcoding a default here since it goes stale.

Prefer a fast instruct model over a reasoning model. This task is filling in a fixed JSON shape from a list you supply, which is not what extended thinking is for: reasoning models bill their thinking as output tokens, take far longer, and some finish a long think without ever emitting the answer. If a reasoning model is the one you want, that works — the status log below reports reasoning separately from the answer, so you can see which one you are waiting on.
Training Plan
The presets are only shorthand: this setting does exactly one thing, which is add a sentence to the AI prompt describing how to structure the days. So anything you can describe in words works as well as a preset does.
Written straight into the prompt in place of the preset. Be as specific as you like about day order, what pairs with what, or anything to avoid. Left blank, the AI picks the structure itself.
Import Data
Merge is right for a first import. Choose Replace to re-import a file you've already loaded — for each day, it clears the existing sets of the exercises the file covers before writing, so nothing doubles up. Sets you logged in-app for exercises the file doesn't mention are left alone either way.
Backup & restore
Downloads a single .json file holding every workout, exercise, preference, plan and setting on this device. This is the only copy of your training history that isn't inside one browser's storage — clearing site data erases the rest without asking. Your OpenRouter API key is deliberately left out, so the file is safe to put in cloud storage or email to yourself.
There is no password reset. If this passphrase is lost, the encrypted file can never be opened again — by you or anyone else. The plain export above never carries this risk.
Restore replaces everything on this device with the contents of the file — it is for moving to a new phone or recovering from a wipe, not for merging two devices. You'll see exactly what is being swapped before anything is written. To add history rather than replace it, use the Fitbod importer above.
This backup is encrypted. Enter its passphrase to continue — there is no way to recover it or preview the file without one.
Deletes every logged workout and nothing else — your exercise catalog, preferences, plans and settings all survive. This cannot be undone.
